claim: GnRH is the primary neuropeptide controlling reproduction in vertebrates.
source: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) is the primary neuropeptide controlling reproduction in vertebrates.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature (Whitlock et al., 2019; Maggi et al., 2016; Brown and Roberson, 2017; Conn et al., 1987).

claim: GnRH stimulates follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH) synthesis via a G-protein-coupled receptor, GnRHR, in the pituitary gland.
source: GnRH stimulates follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH) synthesis via a G-protein-coupled receptor, GnRHR, in the pituitary gland.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations.

claim: In mammals, GnRHR lacks a C-terminal cytosolic tail (Ctail) and does not exhibit homologous desensitization.
source: In mammals, GnRHR lacks a C-terminal cytosolic tail (Ctail) and does not exhibit homologous desensitization.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations.

claim: The LH surge was blunted, but not blocked in GnRHR-Ctail mice.
source: The LH surge was blunted, but not blocked in these mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 4.

claim: GnRHR-Ctail mice showed reductions in FSH production.
source: In contrast, they showed reductions in FSH production, ovarian follicle development, and fertility.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: GnRHR-Ctail mice showed reductions in ovarian follicle development.
source: In contrast, they showed reductions in FSH production, ovarian follicle development, and fertility.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 1.

claim: GnRHR-Ctail mice showed reductions in fertility.
source: In contrast, they showed reductions in FSH production, ovarian follicle development, and fertility.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 1.

claim: Addition of the Ctail altered the nature of agonist-induced calcium signaling required for normal FSH production.
source: Addition of the Ctail altered the nature of agonist-induced calcium signaling required for normal FSH production.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figures 7, 8, and 9.

claim: The loss of the GnRHR Ctail during mammalian evolution is unlikely to have conferred a selective advantage by enabling the LH surge.
source: The loss of the GnRHR Ctail during mammalian evolution is unlikely to have conferred a selective advantage by enabling the LH surge.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that LH surges occur in GnRHR-Ctail mice.

claim: Disruption of GnRH synthesis, secretion, or action can delay or prevent puberty or cause infertility.
source: Disruption of GnRH synthesis, secretion, or action can delay or prevent puberty or cause infertility.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: GnRH acts via its receptor, GnRHR, in pituitary gonadotrope cells.
source: GnRH acts via its receptor, GnRHR, in pituitary gonadotrope cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: GnRHR agonists and antagonists are used clinically in assisted reproductive technologies and to treat hormone-dependent diseases.
source: GnRHR agonists and antagonists are used clinically in assisted reproductive technologies and to treat hormone-dependent diseases (Maggi et al., 2016; Huirne and Lambalk, 2001; Huerta-Reyes et al., 2019; Corona et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: GnRH is released in pulses from neuron terminals in the median eminence into the pituitary portal vasculature.
source: GnRH is released in pulses from neuron terminals in the median eminence into the pituitary portal vasculature.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: The hormone binds GnRHR on the plasma membrane of gonadotropes, stimulating the synthesis and secretion of the gonadotropins, luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH).
source: The hormone binds GnRHR on the plasma membrane of gonadotropes, stimulating the synthesis and secretion of the gonadotropins, luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) (Bouligand et al., 2009; Wolczynski et al., 2003; Costa, 2001; Topaloglu et al., 2006; Cattanach et al., 1977).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: LH and FSH are heterodimeric glycoproteins composed of the gonadotropin α subunit (product of the Cga gene) noncovalently linked to hormone-specific β-subunits: LHβ (Lhb) or FSHβ (Fshb), respectively.
source: LH and FSH are heterodimeric glycoproteins composed of the gonadotropin α subunit (product of the Cga gene) noncovalently linked to hormone-specific β-subunits: LHβ (Lhb) or FSHβ (Fshb), respectively (Combarnous, 1988; Pierce and Parsons, 1981; Cahoreau et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: GnRH stimulates the expression of all three gonadotropin subunit genes.
source: GnRH stimulates the expression of all three gonadotropin subunit genes (Thompson et al., 2013; Thompson and Kaiser, 2014; Kaiser et al., 1997) as well as its own receptor (Gnrhr) (Kaiser et al., 1997; Loumaye and Catt, 1982; Hazum and Keinan, 1982; Clayton et al., 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: GnRH stimulates the expression of its own receptor (Gnrhr).
source: GnRH stimulates the expression of all three gonadotropin subunit genes (Thompson et al., 2013; Thompson and Kaiser, 2014; Kaiser et al., 1997) as well as its own receptor (Gnrhr) (Kaiser et al., 1997; Loumaye and Catt, 1982; Hazum and Keinan, 1982; Clayton et al., 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: LH and FSH regulate gonadal function, most notably steroidogenesis and gamete maturation.
source: LH and FSH regulate gonadal function, most notably steroidogenesis and gamete maturation (Layman, 2000; Abel et al., 2000; Kumar et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Gonadal sex steroids negatively feedback to the hypothalamus to control their own synthesis by inhibiting GnRH secretion.
source: Gonadal sex steroids negatively feedback to the hypothalamus to control their own synthesis by inhibiting GnRH secretion (Smith et al., 2005b; Smith et al., 2005a; Pielecka-Fortuna et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: In females, in the late follicular phase of the menstrual cycle in primates or in the afternoon of proestrus in the rodent estrous cycle, high estrogen levels stimulate GnRH secretion through positive feedback, generating a high amplitude, long duration surge of LH, which triggers ovulation.
source: In addition, in females, in the late follicular phase of the menstrual cycle in primates or in the afternoon of proestrus in the rodent estrous cycle, high estrogen levels stimulate GnRH secretion through positive feedback, generating a high amplitude, long duration surge of LH, which triggers ovulation (Richards et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The type 1 GnRHR is a rhodopsin-like G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR).
source: The type 1 GnRHR is a rhodopsin-like G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) (Sealfon et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: In mammals, GnRHR lacks the intracellular carboxyl-tail (Ctail) that is characteristic of most GPCRs, including GnRHRs in nonmammalian vertebrates like birds, amphibians, and fish.
source: Remarkably, in mammals, GnRHR lacks the intracellular carboxyl-tail (Ctail) that is characteristic of most GPCRs, including GnRHRs in nonmammalian vertebrates like birds, amphibians, and fish (Blomenröhr et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The Ctail plays important roles in GPCR function.
source: The Ctail plays important roles in GPCR function.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Agonist binding to many GPCRs leads to receptor internalization and homologous desensitization.
source: Agonist binding to many GPCRs leads to receptor internalization and homologous desensitization (Sun and Kim, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: These processes are often mediated by the phosphorylation of the Ctail by G-protein receptor kinases, recruitment of adaptor proteins such as β-arrestins 1 and 2, and receptor endocytosis via a clathrin-dependent pathway.
source: These processes are often mediated by the phosphorylation of the Ctail by G-protein receptor kinases, recruitment of adaptor proteins such as β-arrestins 1 and 2, and receptor endocytosis via a clathrin-dependent pathway (Hilger et al., 2018; Magalhaes et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Upon ligand binding, the mammalian GnRHR is not phosphorylated, does not recruit arrestins, and is internalized slowly and with poor efficiency.
source: Upon ligand binding, the mammalian GnRHR is not phosphorylated, does not recruit arrestins, and is internalized slowly and with poor efficiency (Vrecl et al., 2000; Castro-Fernández and Conn, 2002; Willars et al., 1999; Davidson et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The mammalian GnRHR is not subject to homologous desensitization in the conventional sense.
source: Thus, the mammalian GnRHR is not subject to homologous desensitization in the conventional sense.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the previous statement about the mammalian GnRHR not being phosphorylated, not recruiting arrestins, and being internalized slowly.

claim: The receptor has the potential to continue signaling during times of protracted GnRH secretion, as occurs prior to ovulation.
source: As a result, the receptor has the potential to continue signaling during times of protracted GnRH secretion, as occurs prior to ovulation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the previous statement about the mammalian GnRHR not being subject to homologous desensitization.

claim: Some have speculated that the loss of the Ctail during evolution may have conferred an ability to the mammalian GnRHR to broker long duration, high-amplitude LH surges.
source: Some have speculated, therefore, that the loss of the Ctail during evolution may have conferred an ability to the mammalian GnRHR to broker long duration, high-amplitude LH surges (Davidson et al., 1994; Perrett and McArdle, 2013), but this was never before addressed directly in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to speculative literature.

claim: LH surges are observed in nonmammalian vertebrates with GnRHRs containing Ctails, such as birds.
source: It is notable, however, that LH surges are observed in nonmammalian vertebrates with GnRHRs containing Ctails, such as birds (Liu et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: GnRHRs lacking Ctails have been observed in some nonmammalian vertebrates.
source: Moreover, GnRHRs lacking Ctails have been observed in some nonmammalian vertebrates (Williams et al., 2014; Sefideh et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: A knockin mouse model was generated that expresses a chimeric GnRHR in which the chicken GnRHR Ctail was fused in frame to the C-terminus of the murine GnRHR.
source: To gain greater insight into the potential significance of the loss of the Ctail in the mammalian GnRHR, we generated a knockin mouse model that expresses a chimeric GnRHR in which the chicken GnRHR Ctail was fused in frame to the C-terminus of the murine GnRHR.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The addition of a chicken Ctail altered, but did not prevent LH surges.
source: Importantly, the addition of a chicken Ctail altered, but did not prevent LH surges.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 4.

claim: Ctail mice were born at the expected Mendelian frequencies.
source: Heterozygous mice (GnrhrCtail/+) were interbred to produce wild-type (WT, Gnrhr+/+), heterozygous (GnrhrCtail/+), and homozygous (Ctail, GnrhrCtail/Ctail) animals, which were born at the expected Mendelian frequencies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Ctail mice expressed an mRNA encoding the chimeric receptor in their pituitaries.
source: Ctail mice expressed an mRNA encoding the chimeric receptor in their pituitaries (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Ctail females produced smaller litters than WT when paired with WT C57BL/6 males.
source: When paired with WT C57BL/6 males, Ctail females produced smaller litters than WT (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: A minority of Ctail mice were profoundly subfertile or infertile.
source: A minority of Ctail mice were profoundly subfertile or infertile.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Ctail females exhibited fewer estrous cycles per week.
source: Ctail females exhibited fewer estrous cycles per week (Figure 1B), due to an extended amount of time spent in estrus (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Ovarian mass was reduced in Ctail females relative to WT.
source: Ovarian mass was reduced in Ctail females relative to WT (Figure 1C, D), but uterine weight was not significantly altered (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Uterine weight was not significantly altered in Ctail females relative to WT.
source: Ovarian mass was reduced in Ctail females relative to WT (Figure 1C, D), but uterine weight was not significantly altered (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1E.

claim: The numbers of antral follicles were reduced in Ctail relative to WT ovaries.
source: The numbers of antral follicles (Figure 1F), preovulatory follicles (Figure 1G), and corpora lutea (Figure 1H) were reduced in Ctail relative to WT ovaries, indicating impairments in folliculogenesis and ovulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1F.

claim: The numbers of preovulatory follicles were reduced in Ctail relative to WT ovaries.
source: The numbers of antral follicles (Figure 1F), preovulatory follicles (Figure 1G), and corpora lutea (Figure 1H) were reduced in Ctail relative to WT ovaries, indicating impairments in folliculogenesis and ovulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1G.

claim: The numbers of corpora lutea were reduced in Ctail relative to WT ovaries.
source: The numbers of antral follicles (Figure 1F), preovulatory follicles (Figure 1G), and corpora lutea (Figure 1H) were reduced in Ctail relative to WT ovaries, indicating impairments in folliculogenesis and ovulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1H.

claim: Reduced numbers of antral follicles, preovulatory follicles, and corpora lutea in Ctail ovaries indicate impairments in folliculogenesis and ovulation.
source: The numbers of antral follicles (Figure 1F), preovulatory follicles (Figure 1G), and corpora lutea (Figure 1H) were reduced in Ctail relative to WT ovaries, indicating impairments in folliculogenesis and ovulation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing reduced numbers of antral follicles, preovulatory follicles, and corpora lutea.

claim: Ctail males were hypogonadal.
source: Ctail males were hypogonadal (Figure 1I, J) and oligozoospermic (Figure 1K), but their seminal vesicle masses were comparable to those of WT (Figure 1I, L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1I and J.

claim: Ctail males were oligozoospermic.
source: Ctail males were hypogonadal (Figure 1I, J) and oligozoospermic (Figure 1K), but their seminal vesicle masses were comparable to those of WT (Figure 1I, L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1K.

claim: Seminal vesicle masses of Ctail males were comparable to those of WT.
source: Ctail males were hypogonadal (Figure 1I, J) and oligozoospermic (Figure 1K), but their seminal vesicle masses were comparable to those of WT (Figure 1I, L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1I and L.

claim: In females sampled on diestrus afternoon, serum FSH and LH levels did not differ significantly (two-way analysis of variance) between genotypes.
source: In females sampled on diestrus afternoon, serum FSH and LH levels did not differ significantly (two-way analysis of variance) between genotypes ('sham' data in Figure 2A, B), though there was a clear trend for reduced FSH in Ctail mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2A and B.

claim: There was a clear trend for reduced FSH in Ctail mice sampled on diestrus afternoon.
source: In females sampled on diestrus afternoon, serum FSH and LH levels did not differ significantly (two-way analysis of variance) between genotypes ('sham' data in Figure 2A, B), though there was a clear trend for reduced FSH in Ctail mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: The difference in FSH levels between WT and Ctail females sampled on diestrus afternoon was significant when analyzed directly after the removal of the confirmed outlier in the WT group.
source: Indeed, the difference was significant when analyzed directly after the removal of the confirmed outlier in the WT group [t(19) = 2.1, p = 0.0012, two-tailed].
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: FSH and LH levels increased in OVX females, as expected.
source: A second cohort of females was ovariectomized (OVX) to remove gonadal hormone (steroids and inhibin) feedback and increase endogenous GnRH secretion. Under these conditions, FSH and LH levels increased, as expected (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2A and B.

claim: There was no significant genotype difference in FSH and LH levels in OVX females, but both gonadotropins trended lower in OVX Ctail relative to WT females.
source: There was no significant genotype difference observed, but both gonadotropins trended lower in OVX Ctail relative to WT females.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Serum FSH levels were significantly reduced in gonad-intact ('sham') Ctail relative to WT males.
source: In males, serum FSH levels were significantly reduced in gonad-intact ('sham') Ctail relative to WT mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: Both single time point and pulsatile LH release were statistically normal in Ctail males.
source: In contrast, both single time point (Figure 2D) and pulsatile LH release were statistically normal in Ctail males (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: FSH levels did not increase postcastration in males, but the difference between genotypes persisted.
source: FSH levels did not increase postcastration, but the difference between genotypes persisted (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: The postcastration increase in LH levels was blunted in Ctail relative to WT males.
source: The postcastration increase in LH levels was blunted in Ctail relative to WT males (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2D.

claim: Fshb mRNA levels were significantly reduced in male, but not in female Ctail relative to WT mice in gonad-intact ('sham') animals.
source: In gonad-intact ('sham') animals, Fshb mRNA levels were significantly reduced in male, but not in female Ctail relative to WT mice (Figure 3A, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3A and E.

claim: Following gonadectomy, Fshb mRNA levels were increased in both genotypes, but the response was blunted in Ctail mice, significantly so in males.
source: Following gonadectomy, Fshb mRNA levels were increased in both genotypes, but the response was blunted in Ctail mice, significantly so in males (with a clear trend in females) (Figure 3A, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3A and E.

claim: Pituitary expression of the Lhb and Cga subunits did not differ between gonad-intact WT and Ctail males and females.
source: Similar to serum LH levels, pituitary expression of the Lhb and Cga subunits did not differ between gonad-intact WT and Ctail males and females (Figure 3B, C, F, G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3B, C, F, and G.

claim: Following gonadectomy, increases in Lhb and Cga expression were significantly blunted in Ctail mice.
source: In contrast, following gonadectomy, increases in Lhb and Cga expression were significantly blunted in Ctail mice (Figure 3B, C, F, G), paralleling the observed effects on LH secretion (Figure 2B, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3B, C, F, and G.

claim: Gnrhr mRNA expression was significantly reduced in gonad-intact female and male Ctail relative to WT mice.
source: Gnrhr mRNA expression was significantly reduced in gonad-intact female and male Ctail relative to WT mice (Figure 3D, H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3D and H.

claim: Following gonadectomy, the difference in Gnrhr mRNA expression between genotypes was no longer statistically significant, but levels continued to trend lower in Ctail mice.
source: Following gonadectomy, the difference between genotypes was no longer statistically significant, but levels continued to trend lower in Ctail mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Five of eight WT females (62.5%) exhibited clear LH surges on proestrus, as determined by vaginal smearing.
source: Five of eight WT females (62.5%) exhibited clear LH surges, while no Ctail mice (0% of N = 7) surged on proestrus, as determined by vaginal smearing (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4A and B.

claim: No Ctail mice (0% of N = 7) surged on proestrus, as determined by vaginal smearing.
source: Five of eight WT females (62.5%) exhibited clear LH surges, while no Ctail mice (0% of N = 7) surged on proestrus, as determined by vaginal smearing (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Over the sampling interval, LH surges were detected in 93% of WT mice compared to 43% of Ctail animals.
source: Over the sampling interval, we detected LH surges in 93% of WT mice compared to 43% of Ctail animals (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The maximal LH levels measured were significantly blunted in Ctail relative to WT females.
source: The maximal LH levels measured were significantly blunted in Ctail relative to WT females (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: The timing of the surge did not appear to differ between genotypes.
source: The timing of the surge did not appear to differ between genotypes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mice of both genotypes released LH in response to exogenous GnRH, with peaks observed 15-min postinjection and returning to baseline by 1 hr.
source: Mice of both genotypes released LH in response to exogenous GnRH, with peaks observed 15-min postinjection and returning to baseline by 1 hr (Figure 5A, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5A and D.

claim: The amplitude of the LH response to exogenous GnRH was blunted in Ctail relative to WT mice.
source: However, the amplitude of the response was blunted in Ctail relative to WT mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Intrapituitary FSH and LH levels were lower in female Ctail relative WT littermates.
source: Intrapituitary FSH and LH levels were lower in female Ctail relative WT littermates (Figure 5B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5B and C.

claim: In males, pituitary FSH content did not differ between genotypes.
source: In contrast, in males, pituitary FSH content did not differ between genotypes (Figure 5E), but pituitary LH content was slightly higher in Ctail than WT males (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5E.

claim: Pituitary LH content was slightly higher in Ctail than WT males.
source: In contrast, in males, pituitary FSH content did not differ between genotypes (Figure 5E), but pituitary LH content was slightly higher in Ctail than WT males (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5F.

claim: GnRH-dependent Gαq activation was markedly attenuated in heterologous HEK 293 cells expressing the Ctail relative to WT GnRHR receptor.
source: As assessed using a Gαq bioluminescence resonance energy transfer (BRET)-based biosensor, GnRH-dependent Gαq activation was markedly attenuated in heterologous HEK 293 cells expressing the Ctail relative to WT GnRHR receptor (Figure 6A), even though cell surface expression of the two receptors was equivalent (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: Cell surface expression of the WT and Ctail GnRHR was equivalent.
source: As assessed using a Gαq bioluminescence resonance energy transfer (BRET)-based biosensor, GnRH-dependent Gαq activation was markedly attenuated in heterologous HEK 293 cells expressing the Ctail relative to WT GnRHR receptor (Figure 6A), even though cell surface expression of the two receptors was equivalent (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: GnRH-dependent DAG production was impaired in HEK 293 cells expressing the Ctail compared to WT receptor.
source: As revealed with a DAG BRET-based biosensor, GnRH-dependent DAG production was impaired in HEK 293 cells expressing the Ctail compared to WT receptor (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: GnRH stimulation of IP1 production was significantly attenuated in HEK 293 cells expressing the Ctail GnRHR.
source: GnRH stimulation of IP1 production (a surrogate for IP3) was also significantly attenuated in HEK 293 cells expressing the Ctail GnRHR (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6C.

claim: GnRH-induced pERK1/2 equivalently via the WT and Ctail receptors in transfected HEK 293 cells.
source: In transfected HEK 293 cells, GnRH-induced pERK1/2 equivalently via the WT and Ctail receptors (Figure 7A, B) and in both cases was PKC dependent (Figure 7C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7A and B.

claim: GnRH-induced pERK1/2 was PKC dependent in both WT and Ctail receptors in transfected HEK 293 cells.
source: In transfected HEK 293 cells, GnRH-induced pERK1/2 equivalently via the WT and Ctail receptors (Figure 7A, B) and in both cases was PKC dependent (Figure 7C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7C and D.

claim: The Ctail receptor acquired the ability to recruit β-arrestin-1.
source: Although the Ctail receptor acquired the ability to recruit β-arrestin-1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A, B), GnRH activation of ERK1/2 signaling was arrestin independent (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: GnRH activation of ERK1/2 signaling was arrestin independent.
source: Although the Ctail receptor acquired the ability to recruit β-arrestin-1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A, B), GnRH activation of ERK1/2 signaling was arrestin independent (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: GnRH induction of intracellular calcium mobilization was reduced in Ctail relative to WT GnRHR expressing cells.
source: GnRH induction of intracellular calcium mobilization, which depends on IP3, was reduced in Ctail relative to WT GnRHR expressing cells (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7E.

claim: The impairment in calcium mobilization was not caused by the Ctail receptor's enhanced internalization, as the defect was not rescued in cells lacking arrestins.
source: This impairment was not caused by the Ctail receptor's enhanced internalization, as the defect was not rescued in cells lacking arrestins (Figure 7—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 2E.

claim: The three well-characterized GnRH-induced calcium response patterns were observed in individual gonadotropes of WT mice: oscillatory, biphasic, and transient.
source: As expected, the three well-characterized GnRH-induced calcium response patterns were observed in individual gonadotropes of WT mice (Figure 8A): oscillatory (Figure 8B), biphasic (Figure 8C, D), and transient (Figure 8E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 8A-E.

claim: Gonadotropes of Ctail mice showed more uniform responses to GnRH, with extended oscillatory or biphasic patterns that were not seen in WT.
source: In contrast, gonadotropes of Ctail mice showed more uniform responses to GnRH (Figure 8F), with extended oscillatory or biphasic patterns that were not seen in WT (Figure 8G–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 8F-J.

claim: There was no significant difference in the area under the curve (AUC) between genotypes.
source: There was no significant difference in the area under the curve (AUC) between genotypes (Figure 8K), or the maximum intensity of response (MIF, Figure 8L); however, the number of peaks per cell was significantly higher in Ctail gonadotropes (Figure 8M).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 8K.

claim: There was no significant difference in the maximum intensity of response (MIF) between genotypes.
source: There was no significant difference in the area under the curve (AUC) between genotypes (Figure 8K), or the maximum intensity of response (MIF, Figure 8L); however, the number of peaks per cell was significantly higher in Ctail gonadotropes (Figure 8M).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 8L.

claim: The number of peaks per cell was significantly higher in Ctail gonadotropes.
source: There was no significant difference in the area under the curve (AUC) between genotypes (Figure 8K), or the maximum intensity of response (MIF, Figure 8L); however, the number of peaks per cell was significantly higher in Ctail gonadotropes (Figure 8M).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 8M.

claim: Ctail gonadotropes had lower amplitude but longer duration intracellular calcium elevations.
source: When we correlated the AUC with the MIF, we observed a difference in the mobilization of calcium between genotypes, with Ctail gonadotropes having lower amplitude but longer duration intracellular calcium elevations (Figure 8N).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 8N.

claim: WT gonadotropes showed principally oscillatory or biphasic response patterns, whereas Ctail gonadotropes exhibited more extended responses.
source: WT gonadotropes showed principally oscillatory or biphasic response patterns, whereas Ctail gonadotropes exhibited more extended responses (Figure 8O).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 8O.

claim: Gonadotropes of both genotypes responded to a second GnRH pulse, 1 hr after the first, with no evidence of desensitization in either case.
source: Gonadotropes of both genotypes responded to a second GnRH pulse, 1 hr after the first, with no evidence of desensitization in either case (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
